newsitem.title: GERMANY: Zeitler sees German growth at 1-1/4 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Zeitler sees German growth at 1-1/4 pct in 1996.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said on Tuesday that he expected the German economy to grow by "1-1/4 percent or more" in 1996, adding that conditions for growth were favourable.

"Due to favourable economic data and the continually favourable findamental triangle of high price stability, interest rates at almost historic lows and a calm development in exchange rates real growth of one percent for 1996 appears to be the likely minimum," he said.
But Zeitler warned that it was a matter for some concern that domestic demand for investment goods was lagging behind other elements of the upturn, which continued to be driven by export demand.
He hoped that a further reduction in the corporate tax burden could be agreed to help foster such investment.

Turning generally to the issue of corporate strength and companies' investment patterns, Zeitler said he believed it would be a mistake for German companies to adopt anglo-saxon trends wholesale -- such as a increased emphasis on shareholder value -- adding that this could lead to short-termism.
"The (shareholder value) concept should not be used as a justification for a short-term corporate policy....which would mean the long-term interests of the company would be cut short," he said.

He added that the adoption of international accounting techniques at companies also ran the risk of encouraging companies to take a short-term approach by allowing them to incorporate profits which could be achieved rather than those which had already actually been booked.

German companies, which have traditionally put long-term interests above short-term considerations, are increasingly adopting the tenets of shareholder value, which place returns for share owners at a high priority.
